result:
**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first word is always the hardest. It sits on the tongue like a stone, heavy and awkward, refusing to be dislodged. You can feel it there—*begin*—but it doesn’t want to come out. Maybe because beginnings are lies. Nothing truly starts; everything is just the middle of something else. The universe didn’t begin with a bang but with a whisper, a sigh, a slow unraveling of silence into sound. And yet, here we are, pretending that this—*this*—is where it all starts.

II.

I once read that the average person speaks about 16,000 words a day. Sixteen thousand. That’s a novel every two days, a library over a lifetime. Most of them are forgotten before they even leave the mouth. *"Pass the salt."* *"Did you see that?"* *"I’m tired."* Words like dust, settling on surfaces, invisible until the light hits just right. But some words linger. They burrow. They become part of the flesh.

My grandmother’s last words to me were, *"Don’t forget to water the basil."* Not *I love you.* Not *I’ll miss you.* Just basil, wilting in a pot on her windowsill. I watered it for months after she died, long after the leaves turned black and crisp. I couldn’t let it go. Those words had roots.

III.

There’s a myth—maybe it’s true—that the ancient Egyptians believed words had power because they were the breath of the gods. To speak a thing was to make it real. *Let there be light.* And there was. But what about the things we don’t say? The words that die in the throat, the sentences that curl up and wither before they’re born. Do they have power too? The unsent text. The unspoken apology. The *I love you* swallowed back like a bitter pill.

I think those words are the heaviest of all.

IV.

A thousand words. A arbitrary number, really. A round, neat figure that means nothing and everything. You could describe a sunset in a thousand words and still miss the way the light made the clouds look like molten gold. You could write a thousand words about grief and never touch the hollow ache in the ribs where the missing lives. Language is a sieve. It lets so much slip through.

And yet—we keep trying. We carve words into stone. We tattoo them on skin. We whisper them into the dark, hoping someone, somewhere, will hear.

V.

I had a teacher in college who said, *"Writing is just controlled bleeding."* At the time, I thought it was pretentious. Now I understand. To write is to crack yourself open and let the mess spill out, then shape it into something that resembles sense. It’s alchemy. Turn pain into poetry. Turn silence into song.

But what if you don’t want to bleed? What if you’d rather keep the wounds sealed, the scars hidden? Is that cowardice, or survival?

VI.

The internet is a graveyard of words. Tweets deleted in shame. Blog posts abandoned mid-sentence. Comments typed in anger and never posted. We are all ghost writers now, haunting our own half-finished thoughts. Sometimes I wonder if the world would be better off with less noise. If we spoke only when necessary, like trees—slow, deliberate, meaningful. A forest doesn’t need to shout to be heard.

VII.

I’m at 500 words now. Halfway. The page is a mirror, and I don’t like what I see. A woman (a girl? a ghost?) typing frantically, as if words can outrun time. As if arranging letters in the right order can stave off entropy. It can’t. Everything decays. Even language. Words shift meaning like sand. *Gay* once meant happy. *Awful* once meant full of awe. What will *love* mean in a hundred years? Will it still hurt the same?

VIII.

There’s a game I play when I can’t sleep. I pick a word and follow it backward through time, like unraveling a thread. *Night.* From Old English *niht*, from Proto-Germanic *nakht*, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts*. The same root as *nocturnal*, *equinox*, *nocturne*. A word that has carried darkness for thousands of years. Imagine all the people who have whispered it into the void, hoping for morning.

IX.

I used to believe in the perfect sentence. The one that could encapsulate an entire life in a single breath. Now I know better. Life is too messy for perfection. It’s all fragments, half-remembered dreams, conversations cut short. The best we can do is string the broken pieces together and call it art.

X.

900 words. Almost there. I could fill the last hundred with a list of things I’m afraid of: silence, forgetting, being forgotten, the way my hands shake when I think too hard about the future. But fear is boring. Everyone’s afraid. The braver thing is to say what you want.

I want to be remembered in verbs, not nouns. Not as a *writer* or a *daughter* or a *ghost*, but as someone who *loved*, who *fought*, who *tried*. I want my words to outlive me, not as monuments, but as seeds. Something small that grows wild, unruly, alive.

XI.

1000.

The end is just another beginning in disguise. The cursor blinks, waiting. The page is never really full. There’s always room for one more word.

*(Breathe.)*

Begin.
